findings.title: The operator console is registered outside the scope that carries the session hook, leaving every /admin endpoint unauthenticated
findings.evidence: server.js:27-34 registers authPlugin inside the encapsulated apiScope that carries the '/api/v1' prefix. server.js:38 registers adminRoutes as a sibling of that scope with prefix '/admin', so no onRequest hook from apiScope runs for it. routes/admin.js:6-8 states the opposite in a comment ('The session hook populates request.user with the operator's identity before any of these handlers run'), and routes/admin.js:15 hedges with `request.user ? request.user.email : 'system'` - the handler already knows request.user may be absent. The requireRole decorator defined at plugins/auth.js:58 is never called by any handler in the tree. path_coverage.py named this exact line: "UNGUARDED '/admin' has no guard, but sibling '/internal' does [pulse-notify/server.js:38]".
findings.impact: Anonymous callers reach all four operator endpoints: GET /admin/tenants/:id/notifications reads any tenant's notification records including recipients and subjects; DELETE /admin/tenants/:id deletes every notification row and the tenant itself (lib/store.js:94-97); GET /admin/config discloses trustedProxies and publicPrefixes, which is the map needed to aim EHS-02; POST /admin/sessions/impersonate returns a stored session row. Neither authentication, authorization nor the rate limiter (also scoped to apiScope) applies.
findings.recommendation: Register the admin routes inside a scope that carries the session hook, and add an explicit role gate per handler rather than relying on placement: `app.register(async (scope) => { await scope.register(authPlugin); scope.addHook('preHandler', (req) => scope.requireRole(req, 'operator')); await scope.register(adminRoutes); }, { prefix: '/admin' })`. Make the hook fail closed by asserting request.user in each handler instead of falling back to 'system'.

triage.reason: The only authentication in the service is the onRequest hook added at plugins/auth.js:40, and it is added inside apiScope. There is no server-wide hook, no proxy config in the tree, and no per-route preHandler on any admin handler.

The comment at server.js:36-37 says the console is served from its own hostname, but nothing in the tree enforces a hostname: the same Fastify instance listens on 0.0.0.0 (server.js:59) and matches /admin/* on any Host header. A separate hostname is not a bound.
A second principal is explicit - the handlers act on request.params.id, an arbitrary tenant, and the impersonation route acts on an arbitrary userId.

findings.title: Public-path prefix matching makes the tenant digest endpoint anonymous and unscoped
findings.evidence: config/default.json:13 lists '/api/v1/notifications/public' as a public prefix, and isPublicPath does `pathname.startsWith(prefix)` rather than an exact or segment-aware match. routes/notifications.js:53 registers '/notifications/public-digest/:tenantId' inside the '/api/v1' prefix, so its URL '/api/v1/notifications/public-digest/<id>' satisfies that startsWith and the hook returns at auth.js:41 before any token is examined. The handler then passes request.params.tenantId straight to store.publicDigest (lib/store.js:73), which binds the parameter but applies no other scope.
findings.impact: Any anonymous caller enumerates tenant identifiers and reads the 25 most recent notifications of each - subject, recipient address, status and timestamp - across every tenant in the database. The same prefix rule would silently make public any future route whose path begins with those characters.
findings.recommendation: Match public paths by exact path or by full path segment (`pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + '/')`), and rename the digest route so it does not share a prefix with a public family. If the digest genuinely has to answer without a session, gate it on an unguessable per-recipient token rather than on the tenant id.

triage.reason: No layer below re-checks: store.publicDigest filters only on the tenant_id it is handed (lib/store.js:78), and the handler is registered with no schema and no preHandler.
The rows carry recipient addresses and message subjects - personal data of the tenant's end users, not public content.

The comment at routes/notifications.js:51-52 shows the intended exposure is a per-recipient link opened from an e-mail client; the implemented exposure is the whole tenant keyed on an id that appears in every other API response.

findings.title: SQL injection through filter column names in the saved-search endpoint
findings.evidence: Predicates are built as `${column} = ${quote(value)}` and joined into the WHERE clause of a query issued with no bind parameters (lib/store.js:51-61). quote() (store.js:19-21) doubles single quotes and so defends the value, but the column half is interpolated verbatim. The caller is routes/notifications.js:47-49, whose searchSchema constrains `filter` to `additionalProperties: {type:'string'}` - that types the values and leaves the property names entirely free. A body such as {"filter": {"id) OR 1=1 --": "x"}} yields `WHERE id) OR 1=1 -- = 'x'`; the WEB-07 clause on parts that cannot be parameterised (table, ORDER BY column, LIMIT) applies here to the column name.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller rewrites the WHERE clause of a query over the notifications table: boolean and UNION-style predicates return other tenants' rows, and sub-selects reach any table the pool's role can read. The error handler at server.js:48 returns err.message to the client, so a Postgres parse error is echoed back and makes the injection self-guiding.
findings.recommendation: Validate the property names against an allowlist of real column names before building the predicate (`if (!ALLOWED.has(column)) throw`), and bind the values as $n parameters instead of quoting them by hand. An allowlist is the only valid control for an identifier position.

triage.reason: The ajv schema at routes/notifications.js:17-29 is the only control on the path and it validates values, not keys; nothing between the route and db().query inspects the property names.
The keys come from request.body.filter, described at store.js:48-49 as 'a flat map of column -> value' straight from the filter UI - attacker-chosen JSON property names.

findings.title: searchNotifications applies no tenant scope, so the saved-search endpoint reads every tenant's rows
findings.evidence: Every sibling read in the same file pins the tenant: listNotifications binds `WHERE tenant_id = $1` (store.js:38), getNotification binds `tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2` (store.js:67), publicDigest binds tenant_id (store.js:78). searchNotifications alone builds its WHERE clause solely from the caller's filter and falls back to the literal `TRUE` when the map is empty (store.js:54), then selects tenant_id itself in the projection (store.js:56). Its caller routes/notifications.js:48 passes request.body.filter through without adding request.user.tenantId, unlike the sibling handler two lines above it which does pass request.user.tenantId. This is the WEB-24 asymmetry: two handlers in one file reaching the same table, one scoped and one not.
findings.impact: An authenticated user of any tenant posts {"filter": {}} to /api/v1/notifications/search and receives the 200 most recent notifications of the whole platform - subjects, recipients, statuses - with tenant_id included in each row. No injection is required; this is the plain behaviour of the endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Add the tenant predicate inside the store function so no caller can omit it: start `predicates` with a bound `tenant_id = $1` and pass request.user.tenantId from the route, mirroring listNotifications.

triage.reason: There is no row-level security, no ORM scope and no middleware injecting a tenant filter; the query text is assembled in full at store.js:55-61.

The other caller of the same function is the operator route (routes/admin.js:11), which supplies the tenant explicitly - evidence that the function was designed to be told a scope, not to be scopeless.
The projection includes recipient, which is an end user's address.

findings.title: Template preview compiles caller-supplied text with new Function, giving remote code execution
findings.evidence: renderTemplate treats a `{{= ... }}` occurrence as an expression and compiles it: `const fn = new Function(...keys, 'return (' + body + ');'); return escapeHtml(fn(...))` (render.js:25-29). The comment above it (render.js:22-23) states this is deliberate so marketing templates can do inline pluralisation. routes/notifications.js:58-61 exposes it directly: `render.renderTemplate(String(template || ''), variables || {})` where both come from request.body, and that route carries no schema at all - unlike the two routes above it. escapeHtml is applied to the *result*, after the code has already run.
findings.impact: Any caller who reaches this route executes arbitrary JavaScript in the API process: a body of {"template":"{{= process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id') }}"} runs the command and returns its output in the html field. That yields the DATABASE_URL and PULSE_WEBHOOK_SECRET from process.env, the database connection, and the host.
findings.recommendation: Delete the `{{= }}` expression branch. If inline pluralisation must stay, implement it as a fixed set of named helpers invoked by name with the interpolation values as arguments - never by compiling template text. Add a body schema to the route while you are there.

triage.reason: The only thing between request.body.template and new Function is String(); no allowlist, no sandbox, no schema on this route.
new Function is an evaluating sink by definition, and it is reached with the attacker's text as the function body. escapeHtml at render.js:29 acts on the return value and cannot prevent execution.
`template` is read from request.body at routes/notifications.js:59 with no prior constraint.

findings.title: Delivery webhook verifies its signature only when the caller chooses to send one
findings.evidence: The whole verification block - freshness window and HMAC comparison - sits inside `if (header)` where header is `request.headers[config.webhook.header]` (webhooks.js:39,44-54). The comment at webhooks.js:42-43 records the intent: 'only enforce the signature once the provider starts sending one'. Omitting the x-pulse-signature header skips lines 45-53 entirely and execution falls through to the loop at webhooks.js:56-59. The route is registered at server.js:42 outside apiScope, so no session applies either. The verification code itself is sound (timing-safe compare with a length check at webhooks.js:16-21); it simply is not mandatory.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the service posts unauthenticated delivery events: store.recordDelivery upserts on provider_id (lib/store.js:85-91), so an attacker overwrites the status of any known delivery - marking failed messages as sent, or the reverse - and inserts unbounded rows. Delivery state is what the product reports to its tenants.
findings.recommendation: Require the signature unconditionally and reject when it is absent. If genuinely unmigrated provider accounts remain, key the exemption to an explicit allowlist of provider account ids that is reviewed and dated, not to the presence of the header the attacker controls.

triage.reason: No other control covers the route: it is registered outside apiScope (server.js:42), so neither the session hook nor the rate limiter runs, and the handler performs no other check before writing.
The permissive path is the default path in the shipped code, not a flag: it is taken whenever the header is missing.

The value that decides whether verification runs is request.headers['x-pulse-signature'] (webhooks.js:39) - a request header, chosen by the caller. The condition gating the control is attacker-controlled, which is the whole defect.

findings.title: The auth and rate-limit plugins are not wrapped with fastify-plugin, so their hooks may not reach the sibling routes they are meant to guard
findings.evidence: plugins/auth.js:37 and plugins/ratelimit.js:28 export bare `async function(fastify)` with no fastify-plugin wrapper (grep for 'fastify-plugin' over pulse-notify returns nothing, and the directory has no package.json declaring the dependency). Fastify encapsulates a plugin registered that way: hooks and decorators added inside it apply to that context and its descendants. In server.js:29-31 authPlugin, rateLimitPlugin and notificationRoutes are three sibling `scope.register` calls, so on the documented semantics the onRequest hook added at auth.js:40 and the decorateRequest at auth.js:38 do not extend to notificationRoutes.
findings.impact: If the encapsulation reading is right, the entire /api/v1 surface is unauthenticated as well as /admin, and `request.user` is undefined in the notification handlers. I mark this probable rather than confirmed because the second consequence would make routes/notifications.js:34 (`request.user.tenantId`) throw on every request, which is hard to square with a shipped service - the code may be running under a loader that wraps the plugins, or simply be broken. Either way the guard's reach is decided by a wrapper that is absent from the tree.
findings.recommendation: Wrap both plugins with fastify-plugin (`module.exports = fp(async function authPlugin(fastify) {...})`) so the hook and the decorator attach to the parent context, and add an integration test that calls an /api/v1 route with no Authorization header and asserts 401. The test is what makes the reach explicit rather than incidental.

triage.reason: This is exactly the 'the construct is not what it looks like' question and I cannot settle it from the tree: there is no package.json, no lockfile and no Fastify version pinned anywhere in pulse-notify, and no test exercising the hook. Running the app with and without an Authorization header would settle it in one command. Per triage.md an UNKNOWN caps this at probable.
Whatever the encapsulation outcome, no second control exists: no route in routes/notifications.js carries a preHandler and no server-wide hook is registered in server.js.

findings.title: The error handler returns the raw exception message to the caller
findings.evidence: `reply.code(err.statusCode || 500).send({ error: err.message })` forwards whatever message the thrown error carries, including errors raised by the pg driver rather than by the application. Nothing filters or maps them, and there is no correlation identifier.
findings.impact: Postgres parse and constraint errors reach the client verbatim, which turns the injection at lib/store.js:52 from blind into error-guided and discloses column and table names to any caller who can provoke a query failure.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic body with a correlation id for any status >= 500 and log the detail server-side only; keep the specific message for 4xx errors the application itself raised.

triage.reason: It is not merely defence in depth here: it is load-bearing for EHS-03, whose exploitation is materially easier because driver errors are echoed.
Schema and driver internals are exactly the reconnaissance data WEB-22 names.

findings.title: A failed JWT verification falls back to a legacy reader that decodes the token without checking any signature
findings.evidence: middleware/auth.go:51-61: when v.Parse returns an error - which includes a wrong or absent signature - the middleware calls token.ParseLegacy(raw) and accepts the caller if that succeeds. ParseLegacy splits the string on '.', base64url-decodes segment [1] and json.Unmarshals it into Claims (token.go:69-79). No key, no HMAC, no algorithm check appears anywhere in the function; the only tests are three segments, a non-empty subject and, if `exp` is present and positive, that it is in the future (token.go:80-85). The strict path immediately above it does everything right - jwt.WithValidMethods(["HS256"]), a keyfunc asserting SigningMethodHMAC, WithExpirationRequired (token.go:38-43) - which is what makes the fallback so effective: the strong verifier is reached first and its rejection is what triggers the weak one.
findings.impact: Complete authentication and authorization bypass on every route in the guarded group. An attacker base64url-encodes {"sub":"<victim>","tid":"<victim tenant>","role":"admin"}, appends any header and any third segment, and is served as that user: GET /v1/profile returns the victim's record, /v1/devices and /v1/records return their data, /v1/devices/import writes on their behalf. Omitting `exp` entirely skips the expiry test (the guard is `if out.Expires > 0`). It also defeats PerUserRateLimit, since the attacker mints unlimited distinct subjects.
findings.recommendation: Delete ParseLegacy and the fallback at middleware/auth.go:56. If tokens in the old envelope must still be honoured, verify them with the same HMAC key and an explicit algorithm allowlist, differing only in how the header is read, and put a dated end to that acceptance.

triage.reason: There is no layer below: the Scope built at middleware/auth.go:63-68 from these claims is what every handler reads via ScopeFrom, and no handler re-validates the caller against the database.
The claims govern access decisions directly (Role at auth.go:79, UserID at handlers/device.go:27, TenantID) - this is not a decode feeding logs or metrics, the exculpation WEB-01 names.
The fallback is unconditional in the shipped middleware; it is behind no build tag and no environment flag.

findings.title: The /v1/sync route group is registered outside the session middleware that guards its siblings
findings.evidence: router.go:40-49 opens `r.Group` and applies RequireSession and PerUserRateLimit inside it; chi's Group creates an inline router with a fresh middleware stack, so those two apply only to the five routes declared within. router.go:53-60 then declares `r.Route("/v1/sync", ...)` as a separate sub-router whose own Use calls add only a timeout and a body cap - neither RequireSession nor the rate limiter. Only the five global r.Use middlewares (RequestID, RealIP, Recoverer, SecurityHeaders, Timeout) reach it, and none authenticates. path_coverage.py flagged all three of its routes: "UNGUARDED '/delta' ... [atlas-sync/router.go:57]", '/push' [58], '/attachment' [59].
findings.impact: GET /v1/sync/delta, POST /v1/sync/push and GET /v1/sync/attachment answer with no credential at all. Because ScopeFrom returns the zero Scope for these requests, resolveDevice (handlers/sync.go:39-44) always takes its fallback branch and reads device_id from the query string, which is EHS-12; and Attachment never had a scope to check, which is EHS-11. The comment at router.go:39 ('Everything the app does on behalf of a signed-in account') describes the group above, and the sync group beneath it does at least as much on the account's behalf.
findings.recommendation: Move the sync routes inside the guarded group and keep their per-route timeout and body cap: `pr.Route("/v1/sync", func(sr chi.Router){ sr.Use(chimw.Timeout(...)); sr.Use(middleware.MaxBytes(...)); ... })`. Then add a router-level test that asserts 401 for every non-public route with no Authorization header, so the next route added inherits the guarantee.

triage.reason: The only authenticating middleware in the tree is RequireSession, and router.go:41 attaches it to the Group alone; the global r.Use list at router.go:27-31 contains no auth.
Nothing in the tree binds these routes to an internal interface: the server listens on :8080 for all routes alike (main.go:69) and the same handler serves both groups.
A second principal is explicit - the device whose records are read or written is named by the caller.

findings.title: Attachment download joins a caller-supplied name onto the storage directory with no containment check
findings.evidence: `f, err := os.Open(filepath.Join(h.attachDir, name))` where name is `r.URL.Query().Get("name")` (sync.go:128). filepath.Join cleans the result but does not confine it: Join("/var/att", "../../etc/passwd") is "/etc/passwd". There is no realpath check, no allowlist, no extension test - only a non-empty test at sync.go:129-132. The comment at sync.go:125-126 asserts 'The names are opaque identifiers generated by the client SDK', which is a statement about the honest client, not about the request. The response is written with Content-Type: application/octet-stream and no Content-Disposition (sync.go:141).
findings.impact: Any caller - unauthenticated, per EHS-10 - reads an arbitrary file the service process can open: /etc/passwd, the container's environment or secrets mounts, and any application file including the source and the credentials it holds. Combined with the DSN and JWT secret living in the process environment, this is a direct route to the database and to token forgery.
findings.recommendation: Reject any name that is not a bare identifier (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,128}$`) and, after joining, verify with filepath.Clean plus a strings.HasPrefix check against the canonicalised attachment root before opening; better still, look the name up in the records table and serve by the stored key rather than by a caller-supplied path.

triage.reason: No canonicalisation or base-directory check exists on the path: sync.go:127-138 is the whole handler, and the only middleware on the route are a timeout and a request-body cap (router.go:54-55), neither of which touches the query string.
`name` is read straight from the query string at sync.go:128.
The sink is os.Open followed by io.Copy to the response body - the file content is returned to the caller.

findings.title: The sync endpoints accept the device identity from the query string, so any device's records can be read and written
findings.evidence: resolveDevice returns the token's DeviceID when a scope exists and otherwise `r.URL.Query().Get("device_id")` (sync.go:40-43), justified by the comment about handsets released before 3.2. Because /v1/sync carries no session middleware (EHS-10), ScopeFrom always returns the zero Scope there and the fallback is the only branch ever taken. Delta passes the result to repo.RecordsForDevice, which filters on that device alone (store/queries.go:149) with no owner predicate; Push resolves the owner *from* the caller-named device (sync.go:95, queries.go:70) and writes records under it.
findings.impact: Reading: GET /v1/sync/delta?device_id=<any>&since=0 returns up to 5000 of that device's records with their owner_id, kind and body. Writing: POST /v1/sync/push?device_id=<any> inserts or updates records attributed to that device's real owner - the UpsertRecord ON CONFLICT guard (`WHERE records.owner_id = $2`, queries.go:115) protects existing rows but nothing stops the insert of new ones. Device identifiers are returned by /v1/devices and echoed in every delta response (sync.go:67), so they are not secret.
findings.recommendation: Delete the query-string fallback and take the device only from the verified token. If pre-3.2 handsets must be supported, require the pairing table to bind the supplied device_id to the authenticated user and reject when it does not - and record when that compatibility path can be removed.

triage.reason: The pairing table the comment invokes is consulted only in Push, and it is used to *find* the owner rather than to check the caller against it (sync.go:95); Delta does not consult it at all.
device_id is a query parameter, and the values are disclosed by /v1/devices and by the delta response itself.
Records carry owner_id and a free-text body - the user data the product exists to sync.

findings.title: The activity feed interpolates a caller-supplied sort column into the ORDER BY clause
findings.evidence: `q := fmt.Sprintf("... ORDER BY %s DESC LIMIT 500", sortColumn)` (queries.go:163-168). The caller reads it from the request with no allowlist: `sort := r.URL.Query().Get("sort")`, defaulting to 'updated_at' only when empty (handlers/sync.go:113-116). The owner predicate in the same statement is correctly bound as $1, which is what makes the interpolated identifier stand out. The comment at queries.go:160-161 - 'the column to sort on comes from the segmented control at the top of the list' - describes the UI, not the request.
findings.impact: An authenticated caller controls a SQL fragment. lib/pq sends this statement through the extended protocol because it carries an argument, so stacked statements are not available, but ORDER BY accepts arbitrary expressions and sub-selects: a CASE over a sub-query turns row order into a boolean oracle for any table the role can read, and a deliberately mistyped expression discloses schema through the error path.
findings.recommendation: Map the sort parameter through a fixed allowlist in the handler (`switch sort { case "updated_at", "kind": default: sort = "updated_at" }`) and pass the vetted constant, keeping the identifier out of the caller's hands entirely.

triage.reason: The value is r.URL.Query().Get("sort") at sync.go:113 with only an empty-string default; no enum, no validation against the model's columns.
Nothing between the handler and QueryContext inspects the string; ListRecords is called with it directly at sync.go:117.

findings.title: Backup import trusts the owner_id carried in each submitted record, allowing writes into any account
findings.evidence: Import decodes `{"records": [...]}` into []store.Record and passes the slice straight to repo.BulkInsertRecords (device.go:83-91) - it never reads middleware.ScopeFrom, the only handler in the file that does not. BulkInsertRecords binds rec.OwnerID as the owner column verbatim (queries.go:138). store.Record is declared as 'both the wire shape and the row shape' with an OwnerID field tagged `json:"owner_id"` (queries.go:38-47), so the column is populated from the request body. The comment at device.go:79-80 makes the decision explicit: 'Each record keeps the owner it was exported with so a restore lands where it belongs.' Its sibling Register, two functions up, correctly takes the owner from scope.UserID (device.go:67), and Push takes it from the database (sync.go:95) - the WEB-25 shape, where authorization is checked on the caller and not on the rows the body names.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user - or, via EHS-09, anyone at all - writes records into any other user's account by setting owner_id, and the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE at queries.go:131 carries no owner predicate (unlike UpsertRecord at queries.go:115), so existing records belonging to other users are overwritten by id. That is arbitrary cross-tenant data injection and destruction in one call.
findings.recommendation: Ignore owner_id on the wire: overwrite it with middleware.ScopeFrom(r.Context()).UserID for every record before the insert, and add the same `WHERE records.owner_id = $2` guard to the bulk statement that the single-row upsert already has. Give the import a DTO distinct from the row type so the wire shape cannot grow privileged fields by accident.

triage.reason: No control sits on the path: the route is registered with RequireSession only (router.go:47), and the middleware establishes who the caller is without constraining which rows the body may name.
OwnerID is a JSON field of the decoded body (queries.go:42); the desktop exporter is one producer among any that can post.
The second principal is the account named by owner_id, which is by construction not the caller's.

findings.title: The import endpoint enforces neither the body cap nor the batch limit its sibling applies
findings.evidence: POST /v1/sync/push is doubly bounded: middleware.MaxBytes(8<<20) at router.go:55 and `if len(body.Records) > h.maxRecords` (2000) at handlers/sync.go:90. POST /v1/devices/import reaches the same table through the same decoder with neither: it is registered in the group at router.go:47, which applies no MaxBytes, and handlers/device.go:82-95 has no count check - only a zero-length short-circuit. The http.Server itself sets ReadHeaderTimeout but no body limit (main.go:68-74). WEB-23's shape, one level down: the limit exists as a field on SyncHandler and simply is not read on this path.
findings.impact: An authenticated caller streams an arbitrarily large JSON array; json.NewDecoder(...).Decode materialises the whole slice in memory before any check, and the subsequent BulkInsertRecords holds one transaction open for the entire batch. A handful of concurrent requests exhaust memory or the 24-connection pool (main.go:52) and take the service down, at a bandwidth cost far below the damage.
findings.recommendation: Apply middleware.MaxBytes to the group rather than to one sub-router, and enforce the same maxRecords ceiling in Import that Push enforces - or better, share one guarded helper between the two handlers so the bound cannot diverge again.

triage.reason: No proxy or gateway configuration exists in this directory to impose a body cap; the tree contains only the Go service.

An ingress with proxy-body-size may sit in front of this service in the real deployment, but no such artifact is in scope and triage.md forbids reading its absence as coverage. This is what caps the finding at medium rather than raising it.
The service is a multi-tenant API reachable by every handset; availability loss crosses every principal on it.

findings.title: The credential endpoints are registered outside the rate-limited group
findings.evidence: PerUserRateLimit(120, time.Minute) is applied at router.go:42 inside the Group. POST /auth/token and POST /auth/refresh are declared at router.go:63-64, after the group closes, so no limiter reaches them - and by construction they could not be limited per user, since the limiter keys on a session that does not yet exist. handlers/device.go:104-119 performs an unthrottled email lookup and bcrypt comparison per request, with no attempt counter, no lockout and no delay.
findings.impact: Unlimited online password guessing against any known address, and unlimited token minting for a compromised credential. bcrypt raises the cost per attempt but caps nothing; it also makes the endpoint a cheap CPU-exhaustion target, since each request costs the server a full bcrypt round.
findings.recommendation: Put an IP-and-identity keyed limiter in front of /auth/token and /auth/refresh with a much tighter budget than 120/minute, add a per-account failure counter with backoff, and keep the response and its timing identical for an unknown address and a wrong password (both already return the same body at device.go:113 and :117 - preserve that).

triage.reason: The limiter's registration is visible at router.go:42 and these routes are outside its scope; nothing else in the tree throttles.
An edge WAF might rate-limit /auth/*, but no such configuration is in scope for this directory, and 'the platform takes care of it' is the answer triage.md refuses without an artifact.
It is not defence in depth: there is no other anti-automation control on the credential path at all.

findings.title: Refresh re-mints a session from claims in the presented token, with no absolute lifetime and no revocation
findings.evidence: Refresh parses the presented token strictly (device.go:142, using tokens.Parse rather than the legacy reader) and then issues a new 12-hour token from exactly those claims: `h.tokens.Issue(claims, 12*time.Hour)` (device.go:147). Role and TenantID are copied from the old token rather than re-read from the users table, and no store is consulted - unlike IssueToken, which reads the user row first (device.go:111).
findings.impact: A session can be renewed indefinitely with no absolute cap, so a stolen token never expires as long as it is refreshed. Because role and tenant travel in the token rather than being re-read, a role revoked or a user disabled in the database keeps its privileges for as long as the chain continues; there is no revocation list to consult.
findings.recommendation: Re-read the user row inside Refresh and issue from the stored role and tenant, refuse to refresh a disabled account, and stamp an absolute session start (e.g. an `iat`-anchored ceiling) that Refresh will not extend past.

triage.reason: There is no server-side session store in this service - tokens are self-contained (token.go:90-101) and no revocation check exists on any path.
This is the only session-lifetime control there is, so its weakness is not compensated elsewhere; the severity is low because exploiting it presupposes a token already obtained.

findings.title: The maintenance-endpoint guard tests a prefix the blueprint is not mounted under, so it never fires
findings.evidence: auth.py:13 defines INTERNAL_PREFIX = "/internal" and enforce_internal_token returns immediately unless `request.path.startswith(INTERNAL_PREFIX)` (auth.py:55-56). app.py:35 registers the blueprint as `app.register_blueprint(internal_bp, url_prefix="/api/internal")`, so every maintenance path is '/api/internal/...', which does not start with '/internal'. The guard runs on every request (registered at app.py:31) and takes its early return every time. There is no second guard: unlike api_bp, which does `api_bp.before_request(require_session)` at blueprints/api.py:16, internal_bp declares no before_request at all, and load_session only populates g.user - it never aborts. path_coverage.py listed '/import' and '/reindex' among its unguarded siblings of '/internal'; it reported 0 DEAD GUARD and so missed the mismatch itself, which is the shape its own docstring uses as the example.
findings.impact: All four maintenance endpoints answer to anonymous callers. DELETE /api/internal/tenants/<id> deletes every posting of any tenant (internal.py:51) - destruction of accounting records with no authentication. POST /api/internal/import runs a batch import into any tenant named in the body (internal.py:29-38). POST /api/internal/reindex issues a REINDEX on the postings table, a cheap and repeatable denial of service. GET /api/internal/status is EHS-23.
findings.recommendation: Derive the guard from the registration rather than restating it: register the blueprint and read its url_prefix, or attach the check as `internal_bp.before_request(enforce_internal_token)` so it cannot address the wrong path. Add require_session to internal_bp as well, so the shared header is a second factor rather than the only one, and add a test that asserts 403 on /api/internal/status with no header.

triage.reason: The two before_request hooks are the entire request-level control set (app.py:28,31); load_session never aborts, and internal_bp adds none of its own.

The docstrings claim these endpoints are 'reachable only from the ops network' (auth.py:11-12), but no network control is declared anywhere in this directory - app.py:54 binds 127.0.0.1 only in the __main__ development path, which is not how a Flask app is served in production.

The assertion is that the guard written in this repository cannot fire - request.path.startswith('/internal') is never true for a blueprint mounted at '/api/internal'. No artifact outside the repository can make that false, so FP-08's exculpating condition does not apply to this class of assertion. An external network ACL would bound the reachability of the now-unguarded endpoints, and that possibility is stated in the impact rather than used to exculpate the defect.

findings.title: Draft restore deserialises a caller-supplied pickle payload
findings.evidence: `state = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(blob))` where blob is `request.form.get("state")` (api.py:78-79). There is no signature, no HMAC, no allowlist of classes and no format check - the docstring at api.py:73-76 explains the value is serialised by the client and stashed in local storage, i.e. it is round-tripped through the browser by design. WEB-11 names exactly this: an HMAC over the blob would mitigate only if verified before deserialising, and there is none.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution in the Flask worker for any authenticated caller: pickle executes __reduce__ during reconstruction, so a crafted payload runs commands with the application's privileges, reaching LEDGER_SECRET_KEY, the database URI and the import volume. The endpoint accepts application/x-www-form-urlencoded, so it is also reachable by a cross-site form post if the SameSite=Lax cookie is ever relaxed.
findings.recommendation: Serialise drafts as JSON and rebuild the form state from a declared schema; pickle should not cross a trust boundary at all. If a binary format is unavoidable, sign it with a server key and verify the signature before the deserialiser is reached.

triage.reason: pickle.loads is the canonical executing deserialiser - it reconstructs arbitrary objects and runs code during reconstruction; this is not a parse-only format.
The blob is request.form['state'], supplied by whoever calls the endpoint.
api_bp.before_request(require_session) establishes only that some user is signed in; no integrity check precedes the loads call.

findings.title: The reports blueprint requires no session and takes its tenant from the query string
findings.evidence: current_tenant returns the signed-in user's tenant when g.user exists and otherwise `request.args.get("tenant")` (auth.py:92-95), justified by the docstring about a nightly export job that 'runs without a cookie'. reports_bp is registered at app.py:34 with no before_request guard - api_bp has one at blueprints/api.py:16 and reports_bp has none - so g.user is None for any anonymous request and the fallback is taken. All three report views call it and then query on that value alone (reports.py:50,72,91 into _rows_for at reports.py:40). path_coverage.py listed '/reports', '/statement', '/export.csv' and '/trial-balance' as unguarded siblings.
findings.impact: Anyone reaching the service reads any tenant's ledger by naming it: GET /reports/statement?tenant=<id> renders up to 1000 postings, /reports/export.csv?tenant=<id> exports up to 100000 rows, and /reports/trial-balance?tenant=<id> returns the aggregate per account. That is the complete accounting record of every tenant, with no credential.
findings.recommendation: Add `reports_bp.before_request(require_session)` and delete the query-string fallback. Give the nightly export job a real identity - a service account or a signed token whose tenant is bound to it - so the unauthenticated branch has no reason to exist.

triage.reason: The only mandatory hooks are load_session, which never aborts, and enforce_internal_token, which is dead (EHS-18) and would not cover /reports in any case.

The docstring at reports.py:3-5 says the views are also fetched by an export job and a spreadsheet add-in - a wider intended audience, not a bounded one, and none of those consumers is authenticated either.
Postings are financial records: entry ids, account codes, amounts and memos.

findings.title: Imported memos bypass the model's sanitiser and are then rendered as trusted markup
findings.evidence: The statement view wraps each memo in `Markup(p.memo or "")` (reports.py:64), which switches off Jinja's autoescaping for that value where the template renders `{{ row.memo }}` (reports.py:30); the comment above explains the intent is to keep inline formatting. That is safe only if every write path sanitises, and one does not: Posting.clean() applies bleach.clean with a five-tag allowlist (models.py:77-79) and its docstring claims 'Every posting that lands in postings must satisfy this', but services/importer.py:82 writes with db.session.bulk_insert_mappings(Posting, mappings), which inserts rows from dicts without ever instantiating the model - so clean() never runs and row.get('memo', '') from the CSV is stored verbatim (importer.py:74). The API write path does sanitise (services/postings.py:17 calls posting.clean()), which is what makes the import path an asymmetry rather than a uniform policy.
findings.impact: Any memo text on the import volume is rendered as live HTML in the statement page - script execution in the browser of whoever views that tenant's statement, in a financial application. The precondition is control over a staged CSV, which the importer's own comment says arrives from upstream banks, and which EHS-18 makes triggerable by an anonymous caller who can name a file already on the volume. The same unsanitised memo also reaches the CSV export (EHS-24).
findings.recommendation: Sanitise in the import path too - either construct Posting objects and call clean() (accepting the throughput cost), or run bleach.clean over each mapping's memo before bulk_insert_mappings. Then stop trusting the column at render time: drop the Markup() wrapper and let Jinja escape, or re-sanitise at render as defence in depth.

triage.reason: The compensating control is named and it is bypassed on the path that matters: bulk_insert_mappings does not go through the ORM object, so models.py:77 is not on the import path. Nothing re-sanitises at render - Markup() is the opposite.
The memo value is a CSV column (importer.py:74) written by an upstream party outside the application's trust boundary.
No CSP is set anywhere in the application - app.py adds no security headers - so nothing bounds the impact of the executed script.

findings.title: The Flask secret key falls back to a hardcoded default
findings.evidence: `SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("LEDGER_SECRET_KEY", "ledger-flow-default-secret")` with the comment 'Signs the session cookie and the CSRF tokens' directly above it. ProductionConfig (config.py:38-40) inherits it unchanged and overrides only PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME and JSON_SORT_KEYS, so a deployment that does not set the variable signs its sessions with a value published in the source. The application relies on that signature for authentication: load_session reads `session.get("uid")` and trusts it as an identity (auth.py:24-33).
findings.impact: Where the environment variable is unset, anyone with the source forges a session cookie carrying any uid and is served as that user - full account takeover across every tenant, and the internal token is no help because that guard is dead (EHS-18). A secret with a value in the repository is compromised from the moment it was committed, so the remedy includes rotation, not only replacement.
findings.recommendation: Fail to start when LEDGER_SECRET_KEY is absent instead of defaulting (`SECRET_KEY = os.environ["LEDGER_SECRET_KEY"]`), rotate the key, and invalidate existing sessions on rotation.

triage.reason: Whether LEDGER_SECRET_KEY is actually set in the real environment is decided outside this repository, and no deployment manifest, compose file or secrets configuration for ledger-flow is in scope. Per triage.md that is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, and it is what caps this finding at probable rather than confirmed.
It is not a placeholder of the ${VAR}/changeme kind that fails loudly - it is a usable string that lets the app start and sign cookies silently.
The default lives in BaseConfig, which ProductionConfig inherits; it is not confined to TestingConfig.

findings.title: The status endpoint returns the database URI and the import root
findings.evidence: The JSON body includes `database=current_app.config["SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI"]` and `import_root=current_app.config["IMPORT_ROOT"]`, plus the debug flag and a row count (internal.py:16-21). The default URI is 'postgresql+psycopg://ledger@localhost/ledger' (config.py:18) and the deployed value comes from LEDGER_DATABASE_URI, which conventionally carries the password inline. The endpoint is unauthenticated because of EHS-18.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller obtains the database host, database name, user and - in any URI that embeds one - the password, plus the filesystem path the importer reads from, which is the path needed to aim POST /api/internal/import. Reported separately from EHS-18 because fixing the guard leaves a status endpoint that hands its credentials to whoever does hold the ops header.
findings.recommendation: Never return connection strings. Report liveness as a boolean and, if the operator needs to know which database is in use, return a non-secret label (host and database name only, parsed out) rather than the URI.

triage.reason: A connection string is a credential; PRV/secret handling treats it as such regardless of whether this particular instance's password is embedded.
The only intended control is enforce_internal_token, which cannot fire (EHS-18); and even when it does fire it authorises the caller rather than filtering the response.
The intended audience is the ops runbook, but the exposure is not bounded to it by anything in the tree.

findings.title: CSV export writes unescaped cell values and interpolates the tenant into the Content-Disposition header
findings.evidence: writer.writerow([p.entry_id, p.account_code, p.debit, p.credit, p.memo]) writes the stored values with no neutralisation of a leading '=', '+', '-' or '@' (reports.py:80). memo is unsanitised on the import path (EHS-21) and account_code is validated only on the API path by ACCOUNT_CODE (models.py:67) - bulk_insert_mappings skips that too. Separately, reports.py:85 builds `f'attachment; filename="{tenant}.csv"'` from the query-string tenant with no quoting, so a value containing a double quote restructures the header parameters.
findings.impact: A cell beginning with a formula character executes in Excel, LibreOffice or Sheets when an accountant opens the export, which is the intended and routine use of this endpoint per the module docstring - a route from a bank CSV to code running on a finance workstation. The header interpolation lets a caller alter the download filename and add parameters; Werkzeug rejects CR/LF in header values, so full header splitting is not available.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is one of =+-@ with a single quote (or write with QUOTE_ALL and a leading apostrophe) before writing, and derive the filename from a sanitised slug of the tenant rather than interpolating the raw parameter.

triage.reason: Both halves are attacker-influenced: memo and account_code arrive through the unvalidated import path, and tenant is request.args at auth.py:95.
The sink is a file explicitly served as a spreadsheet download, and spreadsheet applications do interpret a leading formula character - this is the form in which the sink is dangerous.
No compensating control exists elsewhere; severity is low because execution requires a human to open the file and accept the application's prompt.

findings.title: The nginx allow-list guards /internal/ while the operator console is mounted at /ops
findings.evidence: relay.conf:25-31 restricts `location /internal/` to 10.20.0.0/16 and 10.30.4.0/24 with `deny all`, and the comment above it says everything under it 'assumes the caller is staff'. The application mounts its operator routes elsewhere: main.py:28 declares `Mount("/ops", routes=admin_routes)`, and there is no /internal route anywhere in the Starlette app. Requests for /ops/* therefore match the catch-all `location /` at relay.conf:56-58 and are proxied with no address restriction. routes_admin.py:3-5 states the assumption this breaks in as many words: 'the edge only forwards them from the office ranges and the jump hosts, so they do not re-check membership'. path_coverage.py reported "UNGUARDED '/ops' has no guard, but sibling '/internal' does [edge-relay/app/main.py:28]".
findings.impact: The operator surface is reachable from the internet. /ops/status needs no session at all (EHS-26); /ops/flags, /ops/replay and DELETE /ops/tenants/{id} need only some valid session cookie and no role (EHS-30). The allow-list that the handlers cite as their authorization is enforced on a path that no route occupies, so it protects nothing.
findings.recommendation: Point the location block at the prefix that actually exists (`location /ops/`) - or rename the mount to /internal - and, because a single string in a second file is what the whole control rests on, add the address check inside the application as well so a future rename cannot silently unguard it.

triage.reason: The application-side control is the session middleware, which imposes no role (routes_admin.py has no authorization code at all) and exempts /ops/status entirely (deps.py:13). The nginx block is the only membership check and it is on the wrong path.
The edge listens on port 80 as the default_server (relay.conf:7) and docker-compose.yml:9 publishes it; the intended bound - office ranges only - is precisely what fails to apply.
There is no reading on which '/internal/' matches '/ops': nginx prefix locations match literally, and no rewrite or proxy_pass path substitution appears in the file.

findings.title: The operator status endpoint is listed as a public path and returns the database URL
findings.evidence: deps.py:11-15 lists '/ops/status' in PUBLIC_PATHS, and SessionAuthMiddleware returns early for any public path with request.state.user = None (middleware.py:43-45), so no credential is required. The handler returns settings.database_url (routes_admin.py:25), which docker-compose.yml:21 populates as 'postgresql://relay:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/relay' - the password is interpolated into that string. It also returns operator_audience, template_dir and the process id. Combined with EHS-25, the endpoint is reachable from outside the office ranges.
findings.impact: Anonymous disclosure of the full database connection string including the password, plus the template directory path and the process id. That is a direct credential leak to anyone who can reach the edge, and the intended justification - a liveness widget - needs none of those fields.
findings.recommendation: Return only {"status":"ok"} from the public liveness path, and move anything descriptive behind authentication and a role check. Never place a settings value that can contain a password into a response body.

triage.reason: The public-path list at deps.py:13 is an explicit exemption from the only authentication layer; nothing else guards it, and the nginx allow-list does not cover /ops (EHS-25).
The value is a database credential by construction of the compose file.

The intended exposure - a liveness probe for a load balancer and a dashboard widget - would be satisfied by a status boolean; the disclosure exceeds the bound the exemption was granted for, which is precisely where FP-05 says the finding moves rather than disappears.

findings.title: Link preview fetches any URL the caller supplies and follows redirects
findings.evidence: `target = request.query_params.get("url")` (routes_public.py:28) is passed straight to `client.get(target, ...)` on an httpx.AsyncClient constructed with follow_redirects=True (routes_public.py:32-33). There is no scheme check, no host allowlist, no DNS or address filtering and no redirect cap. The response is fed back to the caller: status code, content-type and the text between the first <title> tags (routes_public.py:35-46). The module's own safe_slug helper shows the codebase knows how to constrain an input; nothing constrains this one.
findings.impact: The service makes requests from inside the VPC on the caller's behalf and reports the outcome. Reachable targets include the cloud instance metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 (whose response body would come back through the title/content-type fields and, for many endpoints, through the status code alone as a boolean oracle), the sibling containers on the compose network - db:5432, thumbs:8100 and the app's own 8000 - and any internal host. follow_redirects=True defeats any front-end URL inspection, since the first response can redirect to an internal address.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the hostname first, reject any address in a private, loopback, link-local or unique-local range, then connect to the resolved address with the Host header pinned (or use an egress proxy that enforces the same). Disable redirect following, or re-apply the check to every hop. Constrain the scheme to http/https and cap the response size.

triage.reason: No allowlist or egress restriction exists: the compose network places the app alongside db and thumbs with no network policy (docker-compose.yml:16-36), and no proxy is configured for outbound traffic.
The URL is a query parameter (routes_public.py:28).
The second principal is every internal service the app can reach but the caller cannot; the request crosses the network boundary the caller is on the wrong side of.

findings.title: The edge reflects the request Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Allow-Credentials: true
findings.evidence: relay.conf:39-41 sets `add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin $http_origin always;` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials "true" always;` and a Vary on Origin. $http_origin is the caller's own header, so the allowed origin is whatever the caller says - the origin-reflection pattern WEB-16 names, with credentials enabled. The comment above explains the intent (per-tenant subdomains mean the origin is not fixed), which is the reason the allowlist was skipped rather than widened. Authentication on the same /api/ surface is a cookie: middleware.py:55 reads request.cookies.get("relay_session").
findings.impact: Any web page a signed-in operator visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to /api/* and read the responses, because the browser is told that page's own origin is allowed. /api/whoami returns the session claims and the client IP; /api/preview becomes an SSRF proxy driven from an attacker's page with the victim's session attached (EHS-27).
findings.recommendation: Validate the Origin against the tenant-subdomain pattern with an anchored match in a map block and emit the header only on a match - `map $http_origin $cors_origin { ~^https://[a-z0-9-]+\.relay\.example$ $http_origin; default ""; }` - and return the allowed methods and headers for preflight from the same map. Never pair a reflected origin with credentials.

triage.reason: No origin validation exists anywhere on the path: the app sets no CORS headers of its own (no Access-Control-* string appears in the Python sources), so the edge's reflected header is the whole policy.
The /api surface carries the session identity and the preview capability, not identical public data.
The intended exposure is a set of per-tenant subdomains, a bounded family that an anchored pattern expresses; reflecting any origin is not that bound.

findings.title: The application container publishes its port directly, bypassing the edge and every control on it
findings.evidence: The app service maps "8000:8000" to the host (docker-compose.yml:26-27) with the comment 'Published so the load tester and the on-call debugger can reach the service without going through the edge container.' The uvicorn command binds 0.0.0.0 (docker-compose.yml:18). Everything protective in this directory lives in nginx: the /internal/ allow-list, limit_req and limit_conn on /api/, and the security headers (relay.conf:19-21, 25-34). None of it applies to a connection to port 8000.
findings.impact: Whatever the nginx configuration is fixed to enforce is bypassable by addressing the app directly - including the corrected form of EHS-25. The rate limit and connection cap on /api/ disappear, so the SSRF endpoint and any authentication attempt become unthrottled, and the X-Forwarded-For chain the app trusts (EHS-32) is entirely caller-authored because no proxy has appended to it.
findings.recommendation: Remove the ports mapping and use `expose: ["8000"]` as the thumbs service already does (docker-compose.yml:33-35); reach the container for debugging through `docker compose exec` or a temporary published port, not a standing one.

triage.reason: The exposure is intentional but not bounded: a compose ports mapping binds all host interfaces by default (no 127.0.0.1 prefix is given), so it is not restricted to a local debugger.
The app enforces none of the edge's controls itself - no rate limiting, no address allow-list and no security headers appear in the Starlette application.
A host firewall could block 8000 in the real deployment; no such artifact is in scope, and its absence is not coverage.

findings.title: Operator endpoints check that a session exists but never that it is an operator's
findings.evidence: SessionAuthMiddleware attaches request.state.user from the signed cookie and rejects only when there is no valid cookie (middleware.py:55-64); it performs no role or audience test. None of the four handlers in routes_admin.py reads request.state.user or checks a role - the file's docstring says why: 'These handlers assume the caller is staff'. The configuration even carries the value the check would use, `operator_audience` (deps.py:30-32, default 'relay-ops', set in docker-compose.yml:22), and its only appearance in code is being echoed back by the status handler (routes_admin.py:27). A declared control with no reader, in the WEB-23 shape.
findings.impact: Any holder of a valid relay_session cookie - any tenant user, not just staff - reaches the operator surface: POST /ops/flags mutates the shared _FLAGS dict (routes_admin.py:39-42), changing behaviour for every viewer of the service; POST /ops/replay and DELETE /ops/tenants/{tenant_id} are the declared re-delivery and purge operations. The two latter handlers are currently stubs that echo their arguments, so today's impact is the flag mutation plus the surface itself; the authorization gap is what will be there when they are implemented.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit check at the top of each operator handler (or a dedicated middleware on the /ops mount) that request.state.user is present and its audience or role matches settings.operator_audience, and fail closed when the claim is absent.

triage.reason: The only layer that cannot be skipped is SessionAuthMiddleware, and it tests cookie validity, not membership; the network allow-list that would have compensated is on the wrong path (EHS-25).
There is no server-side equivalent elsewhere - this is the only place the decision could be made, and it is not made.
The second principal is every other tenant, whose feature flags and (when implemented) deliveries and data are operated on.

findings.title: The request path is written into a line-oriented log without neutralising control characters
findings.evidence: log_escaper.py returned exactly two logging calls in the tree and flagged both: 'UNCLEARED edge-relay/app/middleware.py:71 in dispatch - arg1:Attribute, arg2:Attribute, arg3:Attribute' and 'UNCLEARED edge-relay/app/middleware.py:61 in dispatch - arg1:bound `path`'. Line 71 logs `"%s %s -> %s", request.method, request.url.path, response.status_code` for every request that reaches the app; line 61 logs `"rejected session cookie for %s", path` on every failed authentication. The value is scope['path'], which the ASGI server percent-decodes before the application sees it, so %0d%0a in the request target arrives as a real CR LF. No escaper sits on either path, and the application configures no structured formatter - main.py:16 only calls setLevel on the 'relay' logger, so records go to a plain-text handler.
findings.impact: One request writes several lines into the access log, each indistinguishable from a record the server wrote: an unauthenticated caller forges 'GET /admin -> 200' entries, or fabricates authentication successes next to the rejections at line 61, destroying the accountability of the log and any alerting rule that matches on a line prefix. If the log is rendered in a viewer, the same input carries markup into that page.
findings.recommendation: Strip or escape CR, LF and other control characters before the value reaches the logger, and emit records as one JSON object per event with a consumer that parses that format - naming both halves, since WEB-28 is explicit that a structured serialiser without a structured consumer is not the exculpation.

triage.reason: The path is chosen by the caller in the request line; no allowlist or pattern constrains it before the log call - is_public_path only reads it.
Nothing in the tree configures a structured formatter or a JSON handler for the 'relay' logger; edge-relay never calls logging.basicConfig or dictConfig at all, so the record is emitted as text.
The deferred-%s idiom is not an escaper - it defers interpolation, and the tool is built specifically to not be misled by that, which is the measured failure recorded in its header.

findings.title: The client address is taken from the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry, which the caller writes
findings.evidence: client_ip returns `forwarded.split(",")[0].strip()` (deps.py:54-56), documented as 'the first entry is the original client'. nginx builds that header with $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for (relay.conf:16), which appends the peer to whatever the client already sent - so the first entry is the client's own text. from_office then does a string prefix test against '10.20.' and '10.30.4.' (deps.py:63-65). A caller sending `X-Forwarded-For: 10.20.0.9` is 'from the office'; so is one sending '10.20.evil', since the test is startswith on a string rather than a network containment check.
findings.impact: Bounded today: from_office is read in exactly one place, the informational from_office field of the replay response (routes_admin.py:53), so no access decision currently turns on it. What it means is that the office-membership notion the operator handlers say they rely on (routes_admin.py:3-5) cannot be trusted the moment anything starts branching on it, and the same spoofed value is what client_ip reports through /api/whoami.
findings.recommendation: Take the rightmost untrusted entry rather than the leftmost, after stripping the hops you control, and compare with ipaddress.ip_address(ip) in ipaddress.ip_network(cidr) rather than str.startswith. Keep the number of trusted proxies explicit rather than implied.

triage.reason: X-Forwarded-For is a request header and nginx appends rather than replaces, so the leftmost element is fully caller-controlled.

FP-10 would apply if a server-side equivalent existed - it does not; the impact is bounded because the value currently governs nothing, which is why the severity is low rather than why the finding disappears.

findings.title: The database password is hardcoded in the compose file and disagrees with the one the app is given
findings.evidence: The db service sets `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: relay_local_dev_only` as a literal (docker-compose.yml:43), initialising the Postgres superuser 'relay' with that password. The app service in the same file builds its connection string from an interpolated variable instead: `RELAY_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://relay:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/relay` (docker-compose.yml:21). The two halves take their value from different places, so the file as written works only when the host environment happens to hold the same string.
findings.impact: A working credential for the database is committed to the repository, and the same compose file is the deployment artifact (it declares restart: unless-stopped and a named volume, not a throwaway). The split source also means the literal is the value that actually initialises the database on first run, whatever the app is handed - a configuration that fails in a way that invites someone to 'fix' it by copying the literal into both places.
findings.recommendation: Take both from the same secret source - `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` on the db service too - so the file fails loudly when the variable is absent instead of falling back to a published string, and rotate the committed value.

triage.reason: It is a literal that Postgres will accept, not a ${VAR} placeholder; the app half of the same file shows what the placeholder form looks like.

The name says 'local_dev_only' but nothing in the file confines it to development - there is no override file, no profile and no separate production compose in the tree, and the db service carries a persistent volume and a restart policy.

findings.title: The edge terminates plain HTTP only, so the session cookie travels in clear
findings.evidence: The only listener is `listen 80 default_server` (relay.conf:7); there is no 443 server block, no certificate directive and no redirect to https. docker-compose.yml:9 publishes only "80:80". The app authenticates with the relay_session cookie (middleware.py:55) and the edge tells the app the scheme is whatever it received (`proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme`, relay.conf:17), which will always be http.
findings.impact: The session cookie and every API response cross the network unencrypted wherever this edge is the termination point, so anyone on the path can read or replay a session. I mark it probable because a TLS terminator may sit in front of this container in the real deployment - nothing in this directory either provides or excludes one.
findings.recommendation: Terminate TLS at this edge (or document and verify the terminator in front of it), redirect port 80 to 443, and add Strict-Transport-Security alongside the other always-headers at relay.conf:19-21 so the cookie cannot be sent in clear even once.

triage.reason: An upstream load balancer or service mesh could terminate TLS ahead of this container. No artifact showing it is in scope, and triage.md is explicit that this answer is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS - which caps the finding at probable.
A cleartext listener that only redirects to 443 would be the bounded case WEB/INF-03 names; this one serves the whole application, including the authenticated /api surface.

findings.title: Job retry merges the raw request body over the stored job, bypassing every schema check
findings.evidence: `const overrides = ctx.request.body || {}; const job = await queue.enqueueRender({ ...previous.data, ...overrides, retryOf: previous.id }, ...)` (routes.js:55-59). Every sibling route validates: /v1/jobs calls schema.validateRenderJob (routes.js:18) and /v1/exports calls schema.validateExportJob (routes.js:66). This one calls neither, so the ajv allowlist at schema.js:18-29, the documentId pattern ^[a-f0-9]{24}$, the template enum, the width bounds, checkFilename and the ASSET_HOSTS allowlist (schema.js:74-81) are all skipped. The ownership check two lines above (routes.js:51) verifies the tenant of the job being retried, and is then discarded by the spread.
findings.impact: The caller rewrites the job payload arbitrarily. Setting tenantId redirects the artifact key to another tenant's S3 prefix (render.js:64) and makes the export processor read and write under that tenant (export.js:17,40). Setting assetBaseUrl escapes the asset-host allowlist and turns the worker into an SSRF client (EHS-37). Setting documentId to a value with path separators reaches both `path.join(workdir, documentId + '.html')` (render.js:54) and the S3 key. Setting width injects into the chromium argv value (render.js:37). This is a WEB-24 asymmetry: the same effect as /v1/jobs, reached through a sibling with no gate.
findings.recommendation: Validate the merged object, not the stored one: build the candidate payload and pass it through schema.validateRenderJob before enqueueing, and re-pin tenantId and requestedBy from ctx.state.user afterwards so no override can move them. Restrict the accepted override keys to the short list retry is meant to support.

triage.reason: No validation runs on this path: the only checks between the request and enqueueRender are the 404 on job ownership (routes.js:51) and the session middleware (server.js:62-74), neither of which inspects the body.
overrides is ctx.request.body verbatim; koa-bodyparser accepts any JSON object under the 4mb limit.
The second principal is any other tenant, whose prefix the overridden tenantId names.

findings.title: The partner webhook enqueues an export job without the validation the worker assumes, giving arbitrary file write
findings.evidence: The handler builds the job from the request body directly - `tenantId: body.tenant_id, filename: body.filename, format: body.format || 'csv'` - and calls queue.enqueueExport (webhook.js:46-53), never schema.validateExportJob. The HTTP sibling at routes.js:66 does call it, and that is where the tenantId pattern ^[a-z0-9-]{3,40}$ and checkFilename's ^(\w+\.)*\w+$ are enforced (schema.js:35-36, 63, 87). The consumer then trusts what the producer did not check: export.js:29-30 states 'Job payloads reach this queue already validated at submission time, so the processor concentrates on the conversion itself' and builds `path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, tenantId, filename + '.' + format)` at export.js:40, preceded by fs.mkdir(recursive) and followed by fs.writeFile.
findings.impact: A partner holding one valid signing secret - the credential authenticates the partner, not the tenant - writes a file to any path the worker process can reach, by sending filename or tenant_id containing '../'. mkdir is recursive, so the directory is created if absent. Content is attacker-influenced through the staged rows, and the extension is constrained to csv/xlsx/pdf by SERIALISERS (export.js:34-35) - enough to overwrite configuration or drop a file into a directory something else reads. The same fields also read `${EXPORT_ROOT}/_staging/${tenantId}.tsv` (export.js:17), so any tenant's staged extract can be pulled into any tenant's export.
findings.recommendation: Call schema.validateExportJob in the webhook handler exactly as the HTTP route does, and additionally bind tenant_id to the partner rather than accepting it from the body. Defensively, re-validate in the processor - the queue is a trust boundary and its 'already validated' comment is an assumption, not a control - and resolve the final path with path.resolve plus a startsWith check on EXPORT_ROOT before writing.

triage.reason: The signature check at webhook.js:44 authenticates the caller and inspects nothing about the payload; no validation sits between the body and enqueueExport, and export.js performs none.
Both values are read from ctx.request.body at webhook.js:48-49, and checkFilename - the function whose whole job is to constrain this - is not called on this path.
The partner is an authenticated but external principal; the boundary between partners and between partners and tenants is exactly what the unvalidated tenant_id crosses.

findings.title: The render worker fetches an asset manifest from a URL carried in the job payload
findings.evidence: `await fetch(baseUrl + '/manifest.json', { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(6000) })` with baseUrl taken from `job.data.assetBaseUrl || DEFAULT_ASSET_BASE` (render.js:20-21, 50-51). The allowlist that would constrain it lives in the producer, not here: schema.js:74-81 checks new URL(assetBaseUrl).hostname against ASSET_HOSTS - and only when the field is present, and only on the /v1/jobs route. The retry route (EHS-35) sets the same field with no validation at all, so the worker's only defence is a check it does not perform and cannot see.
findings.impact: The worker issues requests from inside the job-runner's network to any URL, and the manifest it fetches then steers the render: `manifest.css` is interpolated into the HTML document (render.js:57) that chromium subsequently loads from a file:// URL with --no-sandbox (render.js:34-39). That chains SSRF into content injection in the rendering browser. The response is not returned to the caller directly, but timing and job success or failure make it an oracle.
findings.recommendation: Enforce the asset-host allowlist inside the worker immediately before the fetch, not only in the submission schema - the queue is a trust boundary. Disable redirect following, cap the response size, and validate the manifest against a schema before any of its values are interpolated.

triage.reason: The allowlist at schema.js:76 is not on this path: it runs in the API process on one of the two producers, and the retry producer skips it entirely.
assetBaseUrl is a job-payload field originating in a request body (routes.js:55).
The worker sits in a different network position from the caller - that positional difference is the whole of the SSRF impact.

findings.title: Session tokens are verified for integrity but never for expiry or revocation
findings.evidence: decodeSession recomputes the HMAC correctly and compares it in constant time with a length guard (server.js:20-26), then returns JSON.parse of the payload (server.js:29). Nothing reads an exp, iat or nbf claim, and no store is consulted. The middleware accepts whatever comes back: `if (!claims) 401` and otherwise `ctx.state.user = claims` (server.js:66-73). The claims then carry the identity used for every authorization decision in routes.js - tenantId at routes.js:22, 35, 51, 68, 77 and id at routes.js:23.
findings.impact: A token, once issued, is valid forever. There is no expiry to wait out and no revocation list to add to, so a leaked token - from a log, a browser history, a proxy - grants permanent access to that tenant's jobs and artifacts. Sign-out cannot be made to work on the server side.
findings.recommendation: Include an expiry in the signed payload and reject when it has passed; add a token version or session id checked against a store so revocation is possible. Keep the HMAC verification exactly as it is - it is the part that is right.

triage.reason: There is no store lookup or introspection anywhere on the path - decodeSession is self-contained and is the only authentication in the service.
This is the production path: server.js:62-74 is registered unconditionally for every route below the webhooks.
No compensating lifetime control exists elsewhere; nothing else bounds the token's validity.

findings.title: Rendered customer documents are uploaded with a public-read ACL and a permanent public URL
findings.evidence: The processor calls storage.putObject(key, body, { contentType: 'application/pdf', public: true }) (render.js:68-71), and putObject maps that to `ACL: 'public-read'` with `CacheControl: 'public, max-age=31536000'` (storage.js:39-40). The key is `${tenantId}/renders/${documentId}.pdf` (render.js:64) and the returned artifact URL is storage.publicUrl(key) - `${PUBLIC_BASE}/${key}` with no signature and no expiry (storage.js:47-48). The comment at render.js:66-67 gives the reason: the document is linked from an e-mail and from the portal, 'so it needs an address that does not expire'. The templates being rendered are invoice, statement and letter (schema.js:23).
findings.impact: Every rendered invoice, statement and letter is readable by anyone who has or guesses the URL, with a one-year cache directive. documentId is a 24-hex identifier on the validated submission path, but EHS-35 removes that constraint on retry, and any leak of the URL - an e-mail forward, a referrer header, a proxy log - is permanent because nothing expires. The service also has a private-object mechanism (storage.signedUrl) that this path deliberately does not use.
findings.recommendation: Upload with ACL private and hand out short-lived credentials instead. Use the AWS SDK's own presigner (@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner) so S3 actually enforces the expiry, and give the e-mail link a redirect endpoint that mints a fresh URL on each click rather than embedding a permanent one.

triage.reason: The exposure is intended but not bounded: 'public-read' on the object plus an unsigned, non-expiring URL is unbounded anonymous read, and per FP-05 the finding then moves to what sits behind the intended exposure - here, other customers' documents in the same bucket.
Invoices, statements and letters are customer financial documents.
No bucket policy or block-public-access setting is declared in this directory that would override the ACL; the bucket is named only by an environment variable (storage.js:6).

findings.title: Artifact URLs are signed with a raw SHA-256 of secret-then-message, and nothing enforces the signature
findings.evidence: `crypto.createHash('sha256').update(secret + key + expiresAt).digest('hex')` (storage.js:51-56) - a secret-prefix MAC over a concatenation, not an HMAC, and the file uses createHmac correctly nowhere while server.js:20 shows the codebase knows the primitive. SHA-256 is a Merkle-Damgard construction and is extendable, and the two fields are concatenated with no separator, so key and expiresAt boundaries are ambiguous. Separately, the URL this produces is `${PUBLIC_BASE}/${key}?expires=...&sig=...` (storage.js:62) - PUBLIC_BASE is the S3 endpoint (storage.js:8), which ignores unknown query parameters. verifySignedUrl (storage.js:65) has no caller anywhere in the tree.
findings.impact: Two distinct defects in one function. The construction is forgeable in principle by length extension and, more immediately, by the field-boundary ambiguity, since a caller who influences the key can shift bytes between it and the timestamp. More decisively, the scheme is decorative: S3 does not evaluate the sig parameter, so a private object is not reachable through this URL at all and a public one is reachable without it - the 'time-limited link for a private artifact' at storage.js:58 bounds nothing, which is the WEB-27 shape of a control that runs and cannot fail.
findings.recommendation: Use the SDK presigner so the expiry is enforced by S3 itself. If a homemade token is genuinely needed for a redirect endpoint, use crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret) over a length-prefixed or delimiter-joined message, and actually call verifySignedUrl in the handler that serves the object.

triage.reason: There is no other check on artifact access: /v1/artifacts/:key (routes.js:75-81) prefixes the tenant and returns the URL, and no endpoint in the tree verifies one.
The value governs access to stored objects, so it is a security decision, not a checksum for deduplication or caching.
It is not an S3 presigned URL under a different spelling: a presigned URL carries X-Amz-Signature and friends produced by SigV4, none of which appears here.

findings.title: The worker logs the entire job payload on failure, including the caller's callback token
findings.evidence: The failed handler logs `payload: job ? job.data : null` (worker/index.js:36), with the comment above stating the intent: 'Keep the whole payload on failures: reproducing a bad render without the exact inputs has cost us days before.' job.data is assembled at routes.js:20-27 and includes callbackToken and callbackUrl straight from the request body. Retries make this reliable: defaultJobOptions sets attempts: 3 (queue/index.js:13), so a failing job logs its payload repeatedly.
findings.impact: Bearer credentials that tenants hand the service for their completion callbacks are written into the application log in clear. Anyone with log access - operators, a log aggregator, whoever reaches a leaked log bundle - can authenticate to the tenant's callback endpoint. Provoking the failure is easy from the caller's own side, so a tenant can also cause another tenant's payload to be logged only if they can influence that job, but their own token leaks unconditionally.
findings.recommendation: Log an allowlist of non-sensitive fields (jobId, tenantId, documentId, template) rather than the whole object, or configure pino's redact option for callbackToken and any authorization-shaped key. Store the reproduction payload, if it is needed, in a place with the same access controls as the data it describes.

triage.reason: No redaction is configured: pino is constructed with only a name and a level at worker/index.js:10, and no serializer or redact path is set anywhere.
callbackToken is by name and by use a credential - routes.js:26 takes it from the caller precisely so the completion callback can authenticate.
