The handler is registered unconditionally in start() (worker/index.js:30), which is what npm run start:worker executes with NODE_ENV=production.

findings.title: Headless chromium renders attacker-influenced HTML with the sandbox disabled
findings.evidence: renderPdf invokes chromium-headless with '--no-sandbox' as its first argument (render.js:34-39). The document it opens is written moments earlier from three values the job payload influences: baseUrl and manifest.css are interpolated into a stylesheet href, and documentId into a data attribute (render.js:57-58), all without quoting or escaping. baseUrl and documentId are unvalidated on the retry path (EHS-35) and manifest.css comes from whatever host the SSRF reaches (EHS-37). The value passed as --window-size is `String(Number(width) || 1240)`, which is numeric-coerced and safe, and execFile is used rather than a shell - so the argv assembly itself is sound; the sandbox flag is the exposure.
findings.impact: A renderer bug that would be contained by the sandbox becomes a compromise of the worker process instead, and the worker holds the S3 credentials, the Redis connection and every tenant's job payloads. Attribute-breaking values in documentId also inject markup into the rendered document, which is what the browser then parses.
findings.recommendation: Drop --no-sandbox and give the container the capability chromium needs (or run it under a seccomp profile that permits user namespaces). Quote and escape every interpolated value before writing the HTML, and validate the manifest's css field against an expected shape.

triage.reason: No compensating isolation is declared in this directory - there is no Dockerfile, no seccomp profile and no user directive; the sandbox was the isolation and it is switched off.
The rendered content traces to job payload fields, which EHS-35 shows are unconstrained on the retry path.
--no-sandbox is a common container workaround, but that is a reason it is widespread, not a bound on what it exposes.

findings.title: The Redis connection falls back to a hardcoded password
findings.evidence: `password: process.env.REDIS_PASSWORD || 'orchard-local-dev'` (queue/index.js:8), in the connection object shared by the API queues and by both workers (worker/index.js:14,20). The host and port default to 127.0.0.1:6379 on the same lines, and package.json's start:api and start:worker scripts set only NODE_ENV=production (package.json:8-9), so nothing in the repository guarantees REDIS_PASSWORD is present.
findings.impact: A deployment that omits the variable authenticates to Redis with a value published in the source. Whoever holds it reaches the BullMQ queues: reading every job payload (which includes callbackToken, per EHS-42), injecting jobs that the workers will execute - including the export path of EHS-36 - and deleting queued work.
findings.recommendation: Fail at startup when REDIS_PASSWORD is absent rather than defaulting, the way storage.js:28 already does for ORCHARD_ARTIFACT_SECRET, and rotate the committed value.

triage.reason: It is a usable literal, not a ${VAR} or changeme placeholder; the process starts and connects with it.
The fallback is not gated on NODE_ENV - unlike storage.js:15, which does gate its development branch that way - so it applies in the production scripts too.

findings.title: applyDefaults merges attacker-shaped objects recursively with no key filtering (prototype pollution)
findings.evidence: The function walks Object.keys(source) and, for a plain-object value, recurses into target[key], creating it when absent (schema.js:92-101). There is no check for '__proto__', 'constructor' or 'prototype', so a source of {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}} reached through the recursion assigns onto Object.prototype. Its docstring - 'Merge the tenant's saved preferences under the values supplied for this run' - describes both operands as request-adjacent data. It is exported from the module (schema.js:107) but grep over the tree returns no caller.
findings.impact: If the function is called with request-derived data - which its own docstring describes - every object in the process inherits the injected property, which can flip a truthiness check anywhere in the application or in a dependency. I report it as probable rather than confirmed because within the files I was given there is no call site, and per WEB-23's own triage clause a reader that may live outside the given scope is UNKNOWN rather than an exculpation.
findings.recommendation: Skip the three dangerous keys explicitly, or build the merge with Object.create(null) targets and Object.hasOwn checks. Better, replace it with a schema-driven default application - ajv already fills defaults (schema.js:25 uses one), so a second merge mechanism may not be needed at all.

triage.reason: No caller exists in the files in scope, so I cannot show the path is reachable in what ships - but it is an exported member of a lib module, not a private helper, and I cannot show it is unreachable either. UNKNOWN caps this at probable; finding the caller (or confirming there is none and deleting the function) would settle it.
The documented operands are tenant preferences and per-run values, both of which originate outside the service.

findings.title: No lockfile, and every dependency is declared as a caret range
findings.evidence: All eight runtime dependencies use ^ ranges (package.json:14-21), and no package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json or yarn.lock exists anywhere in the tree (find over the whole target returns nothing matching). The manifest is otherwise sound on the points that matter: private: true prevents accidental publication, engines pins node >=20, and the start scripts set NODE_ENV explicitly. Enumerated key by key per COV-02; this is the one key that carries a defect.
findings.impact: Two installs of the same commit resolve to different dependency trees, so what is tested is not necessarily what ships, and a compromised minor or patch release of any of the eight - or of anything in their transitive closure - is pulled in automatically on the next build with no review. There is also no artifact against which to run an SCA tool or check an advisory.
findings.recommendation: Commit a lockfile and install with `npm ci` in build and deployment, so the resolved tree is reviewed rather than re-resolved. Keep the caret ranges in the manifest if you want the update path, but let the lockfile decide what is installed.

triage.reason: The assertion is a property of the repository itself - no lockfile is committed and all eight dependencies are caret ranges - and no artifact stored outside the repository changes what the repository contains. A build pipeline that installs from a lockfile it generates elsewhere would reduce the drift in that one pipeline; that is a bound on impact, noted there, not an exculpation of the missing pin.
There is no compensating pin elsewhere; engines constrains the runtime, not the dependency tree.

findings.title: The production API task role is granted AdministratorAccess
findings.evidence: tierPolicies maps the 'ops' tier to the AWS managed policy 'AdministratorAccess' (environments.ts:26-30), prod sets apiTier: 'ops' (environments.ts:68, with the comment 'The production API also exposes the maintenance commands the on-call runbooks use, so it runs on the ops tier'), and attachTierPolicy resolves that string with ManagedPolicy.fromAwsManagedPolicyName and attaches it to the role (service-role.ts:44-45). The role is the ECS task role (api-stack.ts:33-36, 46), so it is assumed by the container serving traffic from an internet-facing ALB (api-stack.ts:76-79). The scoped grants immediately below it - grantArtifacts, grantQueue, database.secret.grantRead (api-stack.ts:39-41) - become meaningless once a policy of `Action: *, Resource: *` is attached to the same role.
findings.impact: Any code execution or SSRF in the production API container yields full administrative control of AWS account 000000000003: reading every bucket and secret, creating IAM principals for persistence, and deleting the account's resources. The task's credentials are retrievable from the ECS metadata endpoint by any process in the container, so the bar is a single application vulnerability - of which this audit found several classes in the sibling services.
findings.recommendation: Remove AdministratorAccess from the tier map. Give the API only the grants it needs (the three already present), and if maintenance commands genuinely require broader rights, move them to a separate task with its own role, assumed deliberately and logged - not shared with the request-serving container.

triage.reason: No SCP, permissions boundary or condition appears anywhere in the tree - cdk.json's context (lines 7-15) sets minimizePolicies and checkSecretUsage, neither of which trims a managed policy, and no organization policy artifact is in scope.
The wildcard is not an ephemeral deployment role with a short session; it is the standing task role of a long-running service with desiredCount 6 (environments.ts:71).
This is specifically the production branch: dev and staging use the 'standard' tier (environments.ts:39,53) and only prod selects 'ops'.

findings.title: The production artifact bucket is opened to anonymous reads while holding tenant documents and exports
findings.evidence: When publicRead is set, the construct both weakens the public-access block - blockPublicPolicy: false and restrictPublicBuckets: false instead of BLOCK_ALL (bucket.ts:33-40) - and attaches a resource policy granting s3:GetObject to `new iam.AnyPrincipal()` over `arnForObjects('*')`, i.e. every object in the bucket (bucket.ts:55-64). prod sets assetsPublic: true (environments.ts:64), and data-stack.ts passes it as publicRead (data-stack.ts:29). What that bucket holds is stated two lines above the construction: 'One bucket holds everything the platform produces: the brand assets the CDN pulls, the rendered documents and the tenant data exports' (data-stack.ts:26-27). The construct's own docstring claims 'Public reads are opt-in' - true, and the opt-in is at the whole-bucket granularity.
findings.impact: Every rendered customer document and every tenant data export in the production bucket is readable by anyone on the internet, not merely the brand assets the CDN needs. The bucket name is published as a CfnOutput (data-stack.ts:66-68), so it is not obscure. This is INF-02's exact exculpation clause failing: it would be a public-assets bucket by design if the pipeline wrote only assets there, and it does not.
findings.recommendation: Separate the buckets: a public assets bucket the CDN reads, and a private bucket for documents and exports with BLOCK_ALL. If they must stay together, scope the policy to a single prefix (`arnForObjects('public/*')`) and keep blockPublicPolicy true elsewhere - better still, serve the CDN through an origin access identity and leave the bucket blocked entirely.

triage.reason: The intended exposure is the brand assets; the implemented exposure is arnForObjects('*'), which is the whole bucket. Per FP-05 the finding then moves to what sits behind the intended exposure, and here that is the tenant documents in the same bucket.

No CloudFront origin access identity is declared in the tree, and no bucket policy condition restricts the principal or source; enforceSSL and versioning (bucket.ts:31-32) constrain transport and retention, not read authorization.
Rendered documents and tenant data exports are customer data by the stack's own description.

findings.title: The dev environment opens bastion SSH to the whole internet, and unknown environments silently resolve to dev
findings.evidence: dev declares adminCidrs: ['0.0.0.0/0'] (environments.ts:36) while staging and prod declare specific ranges (environments.ts:49, 62). network-stack.ts:52-58 loops over that list and adds an ingress rule for TCP 22 per entry, so dev's bastion accepts SSH from anywhere. The blast radius is widened by the selector: `pickEnv` returns `environments[name ?? ''] ?? dev` (environments.ts:83), so an unset BEACON_ENV, an unrecognised value or a typo resolves to the dev config rather than failing - and bin/beacon.ts:14 comments that 'a bare cdk synth on a laptop falls back to the sandbox settings', which is that behaviour by design. The database SG then admits the bastion SG on 5432 (network-stack.ts:81-85).
findings.impact: Port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 is INF-04's straight-to-a-finding case, and the host behind it is a jump box with a path to the database. The fail-open selector means a deploy that omits or misspells BEACON_ENV applies these settings - together with assetsPublic: true and RemovalPolicy.DESTROY - into whichever account the ambient credentials point at.
findings.recommendation: Give dev real ranges like the other two environments, and make pickEnv throw on an unknown or missing name rather than defaulting: `const cfg = environments[name]; if (!cfg) throw new Error('set BEACON_ENV to dev|staging|prod');`. Fail-closed selection is what keeps a typo from deploying the most permissive configuration.

triage.reason: FP-05's bounded case is a public load balancer on 443; this is management access on 22, which INF-04 lists among the ports that make the finding critical rather than reviewable.

No NACL or managed firewall is declared in the same repository - the VPC construct at network-stack.ts:22-43 adds subnets and flow logs, no network ACLs - and INF-04 is explicit that an undeclared one must not be assumed.
It would be dev-only if dev were only reachable deliberately; the pickEnv fallback at environments.ts:83 is what makes dev the default rather than an opt-in.

findings.title: The production database is declared publicly accessible
findings.evidence: `publiclyAccessible: true` on the rds.DatabaseInstance (data-stack.ts:60), with the comment 'The analytics warehouse lives in a separate account and pulls nightly over the public endpoint.' The same construct places the instance in PRIVATE_ISOLATED subnets (data-stack.ts:48) and attaches databaseSg, whose ingress is limited to the service SG and the bastion SG on 5432 (network-stack.ts:76-85). The endpoint address is published as a CfnOutput (data-stack.ts:69-71).
findings.impact: The setting requests a publicly resolvable endpoint for a production database holding tenant data, contradicting the isolated-subnet placement in the same construct. Two things stand between that request and exposure - the isolated subnets' lack of an internet route, and the security group - so I report this as probable rather than confirmed: I cannot establish from the tree alone what RDS provisions for this combination, and a single future change to either control turns the declaration into reachability. The cross-account pull the comment describes is not implemented anywhere in the tree, so the setting buys nothing today.
findings.recommendation: Set publiclyAccessible: false and give the analytics account a VPC peering connection, a PrivateLink endpoint or a replica it can reach privately. If a public endpoint is genuinely required, pair it with a narrow SG allowing only the warehouse's egress addresses and record that decision beside the setting.

triage.reason: The security group is a real control on the path (network-stack.ts:71-85) and the subnet placement is another, so the exculpation is partly present - but I cannot show from this tree that no code path reaches the endpoint around them, which is what FP-01 requires, and whether RDS assigns a reachable address for an isolated subnet group is not decidable from the source. Per triage.md this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable.
The stated intent - a nightly cross-account pull - is not implemented or bounded anywhere in the tree: no peering, no PrivateLink, no source-restricted rule for the warehouse.
The instance holds the platform's tenant data; storageEncrypted and a 21-day backup retention (data-stack.ts:52,55) confirm it is treated as such.

findings.title: The artifact grant is issued with the empty prefix its own signature exists to constrain
findings.evidence: grantArtifacts takes `prefix = ''` as its third parameter, and its docstring says why it is there: 'Pass the prefix the service writes under so the grant stays scoped to it' (service-role.ts:48-56). api-stack.ts:39 calls it with two arguments, so prefix stays '', and the statements become s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject on `arnForObjects('*')` plus s3:ListBucket with a StringLike condition of '*' (service-role.ts:57-69) - the whole bucket, read, write and delete. That bucket is the shared one holding every tenant's rendered documents and exports (data-stack.ts:26-27).
findings.impact: The API task role can read, overwrite and delete any object belonging to any tenant, and enumerate the entire bucket - so a path-manipulation or tenant-confusion bug in the application reaches other tenants' documents rather than being contained by IAM. Reported separately from EHS-46 because it is the grant that will still be wrong once AdministratorAccess is removed: fixing the tier map leaves this call unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Pass the prefix the service actually writes under - `grantArtifacts(serviceRole.role, props.artifacts.bucket, 'renders/')` - or, if the prefix is per-tenant, add an IAM condition on ${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant}. Making the parameter required rather than defaulted would stop the next caller from omitting it.

triage.reason: No bucket policy in the tree narrows what this principal may touch; bucket.ts adds only the public-read statement (bucket.ts:56-63), which widens rather than narrows.
The bucket is explicitly shared across purposes and tenants (data-stack.ts:26-27), so whole-bucket write and delete is not a bounded scope for one service.
It is load-bearing rather than defence in depth: with the prefix supplied, IAM would contain exactly the cross-tenant object access the sibling services' path handling can produce.

findings.title: The API container is configured with a wildcard CORS origin together with credentials
findings.evidence: The task definition passes CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN: '*' and CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS: 'true' into the container environment (api-stack.ts:59-60), with the comment 'Browsers hit the API from every tenant's own subdomain and from the embedded widget, so the origin cannot be pinned.' The pair is the combination WEB-16 names: a browser refuses a literal '*' when credentials are requested, so an implementation that means to honour both must reflect the caller's Origin - which is the vulnerable form, not a safe one.
findings.impact: If the image implements the pair by reflecting Origin (the only way to satisfy both), any web page can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the production API and read the responses. I mark this probable because the consuming image, beacon/api:1.12.0 (api-stack.ts:50), is not in this tree, so how it interprets the two variables cannot be established here. The configuration is what is being reported: no combination of an implementation and this pair is safe.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the tenant-subdomain pattern the comment describes and have the application validate the Origin against it with an anchored match, emitting the specific origin only on a match. If credentials are genuinely needed from an embedded widget on arbitrary sites, that is a design question to settle before configuration.

triage.reason: The sink is the application inside beacon/api:1.12.0, which is not in scope, so I cannot show what it does with these two variables in the version in use - which FP-03 requires. Per triage.md that caps this at probable.
CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS: 'true' asserts that the responses carry credentials, so the endpoint is not the identical-for-everyone case the rule describes.
No layer in front validates the origin: the ALB listener (api-stack.ts:82-93) terminates TLS and forwards, and no WAF or origin allowlist is declared in the tree.
